85.title: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
85.hook: a prison at midnight, a river that parts, and a baby carried across it to safety
85.howItsDone: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast through the day, sing devotional songs, and stay awake until midnight, when they celebrate Krishna's birth with bells and conch shells, rock a small image of baby Krishna in a cradle, and break the fast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a rakhi: a thread on a wrist, and a promise back. Your line was a thread can hold a promise. Did you tell someone you've got them? Today, a birth in a prison. Day eighty-five.

It's nearly midnight in thousands of homes. Nobody has eaten since morning. A tiny cradle sits in the corner of the living room, decorated with flowers, and in it, nothing yet. Somebody is singing. The kids are fighting sleep and losing. Then the clock turns twelve, and the whole room erupts: bells, conch shells, clapping, someone crying a little. A small figure of a baby is placed in the cradle and rocked. The fast is broken with butter and sweets. Why stay up for midnight? Because of where this baby was born, and what happened the minute after.
screen: `A CRADLE, STILL EMPTY.` → `THE CLOCK TURNS TWELVE.` → `BELLS, CONCH SHELLS, A BABY.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it. King Kamsa of Mathura has heard a voice from the sky: the eighth child of his sister Devaki will kill him. So he throws Devaki and her husband Vasudeva into prison and kills each child as it's born. Six die. The seventh, the story says, is secretly moved to safety. Then the eighth, Krishna, is born at midnight, on the eighth day of the dark half of the month, as tradition keeps it. That's the word. Janma, birth. Ashtami, the eighth. Then the crossing: the guards sleep, the doors open, and Vasudeva carries the baby through the storm to the Yamuna, which gives way and lets him through. In Gokul, a village of cowherds, he leaves Krishna with Yashoda, and carries her newborn girl back into the cell. Hold on to that girl. She has her own story, and it comes back another day. Tonight, follow the baby. In the morning, Gokul knows none of this. All the village knows is that Nanda, the chief of the cowherds, has a son. The tenth book of the Bhagavata describes what happens next. Nanda bathes and gives away cows. The cowherds arrive dressed up, carrying gifts. And then the party gets out of hand in the best way: they splash each other with curd, milk, ghee and water, and throw butter at each other, until the whole village is slippery with it. In some places the day after Janmashtami still carries that name: Nandotsava, Nanda's festival. Look at the two halves of the night. In the prison, chains, a storm, a king who wants the child dead. Across the river, a village throwing butter for joy, with no idea how close it came. The same baby is at the center of both. The good arrives at midnight. By morning, someone is already celebrating.
screen: `THE EIGHTH CHILD.` · `JANMA, BIRTH. ASHTAMI, THE EIGHTH.` · `THE RIVER GIVES WAY.` · `MORNING IN GOKUL: BUTTER AND CURD.` · then, large: `THE GOOD ARRIVES AT MIDNIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in the dark and wait. If you can, turn off the light, or close your eyes and cup your hands over them. Let it be dark. Breathe slowly. Think of something in your life that feels like a locked room right now. Don't try to fix it. Just wait with it, the way a family waits by an empty cradle, not knowing the hour, but staying up anyway. If you pray, you can say Krishna's name. The bell holds the time.
Janmashtami. Janma, birth; ashtami, the eighth day. The night Krishna was born, kept awake until midnight.
Your line: the good arrives at midnight. Today, when something looks locked, remember the prison doors, and give it one more hour before you decide how it ends. Day eighty-five.

86.title: Ganesh Chaturthi: welcoming Ganesha home
86.hook: clay Ganeshas are carried home with drums, kept for days, then given back to the water
86.carry: welcome it, then let it go
86.tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
86.howItsDone: At Ganesh Chaturthi many Hindu families bring a clay image of Ganesha home or to a neighborhood pavilion, worship him with lamps, flowers and modaks for one and a half to ten days, and then carry him in procession to be immersed in water.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janmashtami: a baby born in a prison at midnight, carried across a flooding river. Your line was the good arrives at midnight. Today, a god who comes to stay for a few days. Day eighty-six.

Pune, late summer. The streets are packed, and the drums are so loud you feel them in your chest. A family is walking home from a workshop carrying something wrapped in cloth, held the way you'd hold a sleeping child. Under the cloth is Ganesha, made of clay, with his elephant head and round belly. For the next few days he'll live in their home. He'll be fed, sung to, visited by the neighbors. And then, at the end, they'll carry him down to the sea, or a lake, or a bucket in the courtyard, and give him to the water. On purpose.
screen: `DRUMS IN THE STREET.` → `A CLAY GOD, CARRIED LIKE A CHILD.` → `THEN GIVEN TO THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Chaturthi means the fourth. Ganesh Chaturthi falls on the fourth day of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapada, and it's remembered as Ganesha's birthday. You already know how he was born: shaped by Parvati, and given an elephant's head. The festival does something unusual. It makes a god out of river clay, invites him to live with you, and then dissolves him. Here's how it goes. The clay image comes home. A priest or an elder performs a short rite to invite Ganesha to be present in it; from then on, it's treated as a guest of the highest kind. Lamps, flowers, and his favorite sweet, the modak, a steamed dumpling filled with coconut and jaggery. Families keep him a day and a half, or three, five, seven, or the full ten. And then comes visarjan, the immersion. The whole street walks him to the water, dancing, and people shout in Marathi: Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya. Ganpati, our father, come back soon next year. The clay goes back to the earth it came from. Behind the whole welcome is an old household rule. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends his students home with a short list: treat your mother as a god, your father as a god, your teacher as a god, your guest as a god. Atithi devo bhava. For these few days the rule runs the other way round. The god arrives as the guest, and the family gets to practice the welcome. Why let him go? Many say it's the lesson itself. Love something fully, and hold it loosely. Welcome it, then let it go.
screen: `CHATURTHI — THE FOURTH DAY.` · `A GUEST, FED AND SUNG TO.` · `VISARJAN — GIVEN BACK TO THE WATER.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS A GOD.` · then, large: `WELCOME IT, THEN LET IT GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold something you love, then set it down gently. Find a small thing near you that matters to you. A mug, a ring, a photo, a stone. Hold it in both hands. Feel its weight. Breathe, and let yourself really like it. Think of what it's been part of. Then, slowly, the way a family walks Ganesha into the water, set it down. Take your hands away. Notice that you still love it. The bell holds the time.
Ganesh Chaturthi. The fourth day, Ganesha's birthday, when a clay god comes home, and days later goes back to the water.
Your line: welcome it, then let it go. Today, treat one person who comes through your door like an honored guest, then let them leave without asking them to stay. Day eighty-six.

87.title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
87.hook: Durga meets the buffalo demon; nine nights of dancing, and on the tenth day the good wins
87.howItsDone: During Navaratri, Hindus honor the Goddess for nine nights with fasting, prayers and songs; in Gujarat people dance garba and dandiya, in Bengal Durga Puja is celebrated, and in the south homes display rows of dolls. The tenth day, Vijayadashami, celebrates victory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesh Chaturthi: a clay god welcomed home, then walked to the water. Your line was welcome it, then let it go. What did you enjoy without grabbing? Today, the Goddess, and the rest of her story. Day eighty-seven.

The buffalo demon is dead. You may know that story already: the gods' light pouring together into the Goddess, the lion, the shape-changing fight, her spear and sword at the end. On the nights of Navaratri, while Gujarat dances and Bengal builds its pavilions, the text that tells it, the Devi Mahatmya, is read aloud in homes and temples. And the text doesn't stop at the buffalo. A few chapters later, two demon brothers have taken heaven. Their names are Shumbha and Nishumbha. Their servants bring word of a beautiful woman alone in the Himalayas. And the brothers make a very bad decision. They send her a marriage proposal.
screen: `THE TEXT DOESN'T STOP AT THE BUFFALO.` → `TWO DEMON BROTHERS.` → `A MARRIAGE PROPOSAL.`

segments.voice: Shumbha's messenger arrives with the offer. The king of the three worlds wants you, he says; all the treasures of heaven are his, and they could be yours. The Goddess answers politely. What you say is true, she tells him. But long ago I made a vow, a foolish one. Whoever defeats me in battle, whoever breaks my pride, whoever is my equal in strength, he will be my husband. So tell your king to come and win me. The messenger can't believe it. A woman alone, against the lords of heaven? He goes back, and the brothers send an army. What follows is fierce. When the generals Chanda and Munda come for her, her face darkens with anger, and from her forehead springs Kali, gaunt and terrible, who destroys them both. So the Goddess gives Kali a name: Chamunda, the one who ended Chanda and Munda. One by one the army falls. Nishumbha falls. And at the end Shumbha, the last, shouts at her: you're proud, but you only win because others fight for you. She answers: I am alone in the world here. Who else is there besides me? And all the goddesses who fought beside her flow back into her body, and she faces him as one. Then she wins. Nava means nine. Ratri means night. Navaratri. The text is read through these nights, and some households time it to finish by the tenth day, Vijayadashami, the victory. Notice the shape of today's story. She keeps her word. She tells the truth about the terms. And when she's accused of borrowing her strength, she shows that every form was hers. Nine nights, then the dawn.
screen: `A PROPOSAL, AND A VOW.` · `KALI SPRINGS FROM HER FOREHEAD.` · `WHO ELSE IS THERE BESIDES ME?` · `NAVA, NINE. RATRI, NIGHT.` · then, large: `NINE NIGHTS, THEN THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one small thing you won't let win tonight. Sit, and breathe out long. This time, pick something that likes to bargain. The offer that sounds reasonable. Just one more episode. I'll start tomorrow. Skip it, just this once. Name it, quietly, just to yourself. Then answer it the way she answered the messenger: politely, and with your own terms. Not tonight. You don't need to win forever. Just tonight. One night of nine. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri. Nava, nine; ratri, night. Nine nights of the Goddess, and a tenth day of victory.
Your line: nine nights, then the dawn. Tonight, when that small thing shows up, say no to it once. Just once. Count it as night one. Day eighty-seven.

88.title: Diwali: the row of lamps
88.hook: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way
88.howItsDone: At Diwali, Hindus clean and decorate their homes, draw rangoli at the door, light rows of clay oil lamps on the new-moon night of Kartika, worship Lakshmi, open new account books, share sweets and visit family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri: the Goddess, the buffalo demon, and nine long nights. Your line was nine nights, then the dawn. What did you say no to? Today, the darkest night of the month, and a row of little lamps. Day eighty-eight.

You've heard Diwali's great story: Rama coming home to Ayodhya after fourteen years in the forest, and a city lighting lamps to show him the way. Tonight, look at the lamps themselves. It's the new-moon night of the month of Kartika, in autumn. No moon at all. And on every windowsill, every doorstep, every railing, there's a small clay dish of oil with a cotton wick. Dozens of them. Hundreds, on a single street. Somebody's grandmother has been on her knees since the afternoon, drawing a pattern in colored powder at the front door. The door is wide open. Somebody is expected.
screen: `THE NEW-MOON NIGHT.` → `A LAMP ON EVERY SILL.` → `THE DOOR IS WIDE OPEN.`

segments.voice: The word first. Diwali is the everyday form of the Sanskrit Deepavali. Deepa is a lamp. Avali is a row. A row of lamps. That's the whole festival in two words. Not one big light, a row of small ones, each one ordinary, each one a clay dish you could hold in your palm. And the lamps come on the darkest night on purpose. The new moon of Kartika. If you wanted to show light winning, you'd pick exactly this night. Now, who is expected? Rama, in the Ramayana's story. And in many homes, on the main night, Lakshmi too, the Goddess of wealth and good fortune, of plenty in every sense. Families clean the house from top to bottom in the days before, because the tradition says she comes to homes that are clean, bright and open. They draw rangoli, those patterns of colored powder, at the threshold. Some paint small footprints walking in, as if she's already on her way. They leave doors and windows open and lamps burning so she can find the house. Shopkeepers close their old account books and open new ones with a prayer. So the whole night is an act of welcome. A clean house. A lit path. An open door. Look at who the lamps are for. You can see your own house without them. The lamps are for someone coming from outside, in the dark, looking for the way. Light the way home.
screen: `DEEPA, A LAMP. AVALI, A ROW.` · `THE DARKEST NIGHT, ON PURPOSE.` · `A CLEAN HOUSE, AN OPEN DOOR.` · `THE LAMPS ARE FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` · then, large: `LIGHT THE WAY HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light one light, and think of who you'd guide home. If you can, light a candle, or switch on one small lamp and turn the others off. If you can't, picture a clay lamp on your windowsill. Watch the flame. Breathe. Now think of the people who come home to you, or the ones you come home to. A partner on a late shift. A kid walking back from school. A parent you visit on Sundays. Picture your small light at the door, already lit, when they arrive. The bell holds the time.
Diwali. From Deepavali, a row of lamps, lit on the darkest night of Kartika for someone coming home.
Your line: light the way home. Today, leave one light on for someone who'll come in after you, or be at the door when they do. Day eighty-eight.

89.title: Holi: the festival of colors
89.hook: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
89.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
89.howItsDone: In Braj, around Mathura and Vrindavan, Holi is celebrated for days with songs of Krishna and Radha, colors thrown in temples and streets, and in Barsana the playful Lathmar Holi, where women meet the men of Nandgaon with sticks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali: a row of lamps on the darkest night, and an open door. Your line was light the way home. Who got your message? Today, Holi again, and the other story behind the colors. Day eighty-nine.

Last time, Holi began with a fire: Prahlad walking out of the flames unharmed, and a bonfire lit every year to remember it. That's the night before. But ask someone from Mathura or Vrindavan, the country where Krishna grew up, why people throw colors the next morning, and you may get a different answer, with a grin. A little boy, dark as a rain cloud, is standing in front of his mother, upset. He's looked at the girl he loves, and she's fair, and he's not. And he wants to know why he has to be the different one.
screen: `THE FIRE WAS THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `A BOY DARK AS A RAIN CLOUD.` → `WHY AM I THE DIFFERENT ONE?`

segments.voice: The boy is Krishna. The girl is Radha. The mother is Yashoda, and she's heard this complaint before. So, the story goes, she tells him: go and color Radha's face, any color you like, and then you'll match. And he does. He runs off, finds Radha and her friends, and smears color on her cheeks. And the friends, of course, fight back. That's the game people say Holi still plays, especially in Braj, the region around Mathura and Vrindavan where Krishna's childhood stories are set. There, Holi runs for days. In the town of Barsana, remembered as Radha's village, there's a famous version: the men of Krishna's village, Nandgaon, come to play colors, and the women meet them with long sticks, laughing, and the men hide behind shields. It's called Lathmar Holi, stick Holi, and it's a joke the two villages have been playing on each other for generations. An honest note. This story of the color is told in songs and in Braj, not in the old Sanskrit texts. The Bhagavata Purana tells of Krishna and the cowherd girls, but not this afternoon with Yashoda. Still, look at what the story does. A boy feels different, and the answer isn't to change him. It's to make everyone the same color for a day. Nobody can tell who was fair and who was dark, who's rich, who's from the next village. Krishna and Radha, and everyone else, all smeared together.
screen: `GO AND COLOR HER FACE.` · `BRAJ PLAYS FOR DAYS.` · `THE WOMEN OF BARSANA HAVE STICKS.` · `TOLD IN SONGS, NOT THE OLD TEXTS.` · then, large: `EVERYONE'S THE SAME COLOR TODAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one small grudge, the Braj way. Sit, and breathe. Think of a small difference that's been standing between you and someone. You think they look down on you. Or you've been a bit proud with them. Picture yourself walking up to them with a handful of bright powder, pink or green or yellow, and gently marking their cheek. Then picture them doing it back. Now you match. Breathe, and let the grudge go the color of everything else. The bell holds the time.
Holi. The festival of colors. In Braj, the day Krishna colored Radha's face, and everyone joined in.
Your line: everyone's the same color today. Today, find one thing you have in common with someone you usually feel different from, and say it to them. Day eighty-nine.

90.title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
90.hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
90.tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
90.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, keep a night-long vigil in Shiva temples, pour water, milk and bilva leaves over the lingam, and chant Om Namah Shivaya; many temple carvings show Shiva appearing from the pillar of light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holi in Braj: Krishna coloring Radha's face so they'd match. Your line was everyone's the same color today. What did you find in common? Today, Shiva's night again, and a pillar with no end. Day ninety.

Two gods are having an argument. Brahma, the creator, says: I made everything, so I'm the greatest. Vishnu, the preserver, says: I hold everything together, so I am. It's an argument you could hear at any dinner table: who matters most. And it's getting heated. Then, between them, out of nowhere, a column of fire bursts up out of the ground. It rises past the clouds. It goes down past anything they can see. It has no top and no bottom. And both of them stop talking.
screen: `WHO IS THE GREATEST?` → `A COLUMN OF FIRE.` → `NO TOP, NO BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: This story is told in the Shiva Purana, and in others too. The two gods make a deal: whoever finds the end of the pillar wins. Vishnu becomes a boar and starts digging down. Brahma becomes a swan and flies up. They go for what the story calls ages. Vishnu digs and digs, and never reaches the bottom. He comes back and says, honestly: I couldn't find it. Brahma flies and flies, and never reaches the top. On the way he sees a flower drifting down, and in many tellings, he takes it back as proof and claims he found the top. He didn't. Then the pillar opens, and Shiva steps out of it. The light was him all along. In the tellings, Vishnu is honored for his honesty, and Brahma is rebuked for the lie. This is one of the stories people tell about the lingam, the rounded stone at the heart of a Shiva temple. Some understand it as a small image of that pillar of light: no beginning, no end. And some say this is the night it happened, the great night of Shiva. Others remember his wedding to Parvati, or his cosmic dance, on this night. Households hold these reasons side by side. Now look at what the story is doing. The argument was about who was biggest. The answer was something so big that neither of them could measure it. The only right response was to stop, and pay attention. Stay awake for what matters.
screen: `A BOAR DIGS, A SWAN FLIES.` · `NEITHER FINDS THE END.` · `THE PILLAR OPENS: SHIVA.` · `THE LINGAM, A PILLAR OF LIGHT.` · then, large: `STAY AWAKE FOR WHAT MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: three breaths longer than you want to. Sit, and let the breath come and go. Picture the pillar of light, rising above you and going down below you, farther than you can follow. You don't have to reach the end of it. Just stay with it. When the voice comes that says, that's enough, take three more breaths. No boar, no swan. Just staying. The bell holds the time.
Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva. For many, the night the pillar of light appeared, with no top and no bottom.
Your line: stay awake for what matters. Today, the next time an argument turns into who matters most, stop, and notice something bigger than both of you. Day ninety.

original.note: Sanskrit: the emergence from the linga, the name for this story and its temple image.

trapdoor: what you thought: a night to honor Shiva.
what it means: for many, the night a pillar of light with no end silenced an argument about who was greatest.
what a scholar hears: the Lingodbhava story, told in the Shiva Purana and other Puranas, carved on the back wall of many South Indian Shiva temples.

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Vidyeshvara Samhita (the pillar of fire, Brahma and Vishnu)

91.title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
91.hook: a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist, and he promises to look after her
91.carry: a thread can hold a promise
91.tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
91.howItsDone: On Raksha Bandhan sisters tie rakhis on brothers, and in many regions family priests tie protective threads on the people they serve; the thread is also tied between friends, cousins and neighbors as a sign of care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shivaratri: a pillar of light with no top and no bottom. Your line was stay awake for what matters. When did you stop and notice something bigger? Today, the thread again, and where it came from. Day ninety-one.

Some of the stories told about the protective thread aren't about a brother and a sister at all. There's a king of the gods, going out to a war he's losing. And there's his wife, who won't let him go empty-handed. And much later, there's a province about to be split in two, where people walk into the street and tie threads on strangers. The rakhi you see in shop windows each summer, glittering on cardboard, has a longer, stranger history than the sibling ritual alone.
screen: `NOT ALWAYS A BROTHER AND SISTER.` → `A KING OF THE GODS AT WAR.` → `A PROVINCE ABOUT TO SPLIT.`

segments.voice: First, the king. A story told in the Bhavishya Purana, and repeated at many rakhi ceremonies, says that Indra, king of the gods, was being beaten by the demons. His wife, Shachi, also called Indrani, prepared a protective thread, blessed with sacred words, and tied it on his wrist on the full moon of Shravana. He went back into battle and won. So in this story the thread is tied by a wife on a husband, before a fight. Second, the priests. In many parts of India, on this same full moon, a family priest ties a protective thread on the wrists of the people he serves. The thread was never only one relationship. It's a kind of blessing you can put on anyone you want to keep safe. Third, and closer to our time. In 1905, the British government divided the province of Bengal. On the day the division took effect, the poet Rabindranath Tagore called on people to tie rakhis on one another, Hindus and Muslims alike, as a sign that the people of Bengal would not be split. People walked through Calcutta tying threads on neighbors and strangers. So the thread has been tied by a wife, by a priest, by a stranger, and by a sister. The one thing that stays the same is the promise inside it. And that's the week. A birth at midnight, a clay god let go, the Goddess's nine nights, the open door of Diwali, colors in Braj, a pillar of light, and a thread.
screen: `INDRANI TIES IT ON INDRA.` · `A PRIEST TIES IT ON HIS PEOPLE.` · `1905: THREADS ON STRANGERS.` · `THE PROMISE STAYS THE SAME.` · then, large: `A THREAD CAN HOLD A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one person you'd protect, and this time, go wider. Sit, and breathe. Let the first face come, maybe the one from last time. Then let a second face come, someone who isn't family. A coworker going through something. A neighbor who lives alone. Someone you disagree with. Picture tying a thread on their wrist too. Say inside: I'd look out for you. Stay with both faces for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Rakhi. The thread of protection, tied by a wife, a priest, a stranger, a sister. Always holding a promise.
Your line: a thread can hold a promise. Today, do one small protective thing for someone outside your family: check in, walk them out, speak up for them. Day ninety-one.

original.note: Sanskrit and Hindi: raksha, protection, and bandhan, a tie or bond.

trapdoor: what you thought: a festival for brothers and sisters.
what it means: a protective thread that can go on anyone you'd keep safe: a husband, a patron, a stranger, a brother.
what a scholar hears: Indrani's thread in the Bhavishya Purana; the priest's rakshasutra; Tagore's Raksha Bandhan of 1905 against the partition of Bengal.
